claim.pdf_says:
15.10.2   General format

FUNCTION  ASIN  ( argument-1 )      [FUNCTION and ASIN are both UNDERLINED in the printed general format]
claim.why_it_matters: Underlining in a general format is normative notation (5.2.6): an underlined word is a REQUIRED word. The transcription drops the underline on both FUNCTION and ASIN and renders the format as inline code. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 34152. Adjacent formats in the same clause do preserve it (`<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ATAN</u>` at line 34190), so the required-word marking is inconsistent within a two-page span.

verdict.reasoning:
Independently confirmed against a 300-dpi render of PDF page 849 (E:/Temp/specrecon/v849/spec_p849.png), plus a 1.8x crop of the general-format line (crop_format.png). What I see printed: the words FUNCTION and ASIN each carry their own horizontal rule beneath them, with a visible gap at the inter-word space (two separate word underlines, not one continuous rule), and NO rule beneath '( argument-1 )'. The printed line reads 'FUNCTION  ASIN  ( argument-1 )' with the first two words underlined. The claim quotes the PDF accurately.

The markdown quote is also accurate: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 34152 is exactly '`FUNCTION ASIN ( argument-1 )`' -- backtick inline code, no <u> markup, no other underline encoding. Verified both by grep on the source file and by the extracted page slice E:/Temp/specrecon/v849/page-849.md line 21.

Refutation attempts, all of which fail:
(1) 'The underline is present, just encoded differently.' It is not. Backticks are demonstrably NOT this transcription's encoding for underlining -- the identical construct is written '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ABS</u> ( argument-1 )' at line 34026 (15.7.2), '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ANNUITY</u> ...' at line 34102 (15.9.2), and '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ATAN</u> ...' at line 34190 (15.11.2). The document has an established <u> convention for exactly this markup and does not use it here.
(2) 'It is only formatting / does not change meaning.' It does change meaning, and the transcription itself supplies the proof: line 2631 states that keywords 'are shown in uppercase and underlined in general formats. They are required...', and line 2644 states that optional words 'are shown in uppercase and not underlined in general formats. They may be written to add clarity.' An unmarked uppercase word in a general format therefore reads as OPTIONAL. Stripping the underline from FUNCTION and ASIN inverts their normative status from required to optional -- a reader reconstructing the syntax from the transcription would conclude both words may be omitted, which is not legal COBOL. This is normative content loss, not typography.
(3) 'Reflow / page-break furniture / hyphenation.' None apply; the format is a single short line wholly contained on page 849 in both sources.

The finding is real. The claim's supporting argument is imprecise on two points, corrected below.
verdict.corrected_description:
CONFIRMED with corrections to the claim's framing. The substance is right: PDF page 849, clause 15.10.2 prints 'FUNCTION  ASIN  ( argument-1 )' with separate underlines under FUNCTION and under ASIN (visually verified at 1.8x; the parenthesized argument is not underlined), while specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 34152 renders it as unmarked inline code '`FUNCTION ASIN ( argument-1 )`', losing the required-word marking that 8.3.1.1 (lines 2631/2644) makes normative.

Two corrections:
(a) The cited counter-example is in a DIFFERENT clause, not 'the same clause'. '<u>FUNCTION</u> <u>ATAN</u>' at line 34190 is clause 15.11.2 on page 850. The nearest same-page/same-clause context is 15.10 itself, which contains only this one format.
(b) It is NOT true that the adjacent formats uniformly preserve the underline -- the inconsistency is wider and runs in both directions. Across five consecutive intrinsic-function clauses: 15.7.2 ABS (34026) uses <u>; 15.8.2 ACOS (34068) drops it and uses a FENCED CODE BLOCK; 15.9.2 ANNUITY (34102) uses <u>; 15.10.2 ASIN (34152) drops it and uses INLINE code; 15.11.2 ATAN (34190) uses <u>. A survey of every 'FUNCTION ...' general-format line in clause 15 shows roughly 20 formats using <u>, roughly 20 using backtick code, and the majority as unmarked plain text.

Therefore this page-849 item is a genuine, individually-verified instance of a SYSTEMIC clause-15 defect (three competing renderings of the same normative construct) rather than a one-off local slip. Fixing it should be scoped as a clause-15 sweep to the <u> convention, with ACOS (15.8.2, line 34068) as the immediately adjacent sibling, not as a single-line patch at 34152.
